general_rules.name: chronological_reversal

general_rules.transformation_function: Identify all temporal references (dates, times, 'will', 'has', 'planned', etc.). general_rules.output_change_description: The answer must reflect the reversed timeline. This is the week when the prime minister's past, present and future collide. At 10:30 this morning, Rishi Sunak will sit down in a windowless room in west London and begin several hours of answering questions live on television and under oath. Mr Sunak's interrogation at the Covid inquiry will scrutinise his time as chancellor during the pandemic. Furlough, lockdowns and his Eat Out To Help Out scheme are all topics central to his role in government back then. Key topics that were central to his role are mentioned here. And witness after recent witness have lined up to say they knew nothing about the scheme until it was about to be announced. As Mr Sunak is questioned by Hugo Keith KC, three-and-a-half miles away in Parliament, Conservative MPs will gather to debate his plan to send some migrants to Rwanda. At 12:00 - while Mr Sunak is away from his mobile phone - five groups of Tory MPs will file into the Thatcher Room in the Palace of Westminster:

Under discussion will be the government's latest plan to send migrants to Rwanda, which will go to a vote on Tuesday evening. The MPs will listen to the verdict of the veteran Conservative MP Sir Bill Cash's so-called star chamber - a panel of lawyers that have assessed the proposed legislation. We already have a sense of what it thinks. Sir Bill wrote in the Sunday Telegraph that "at present" the wording of the Rwanda Bill is not "sufficiently watertight to meet the government's policy objectives". Their written conclusions could be published on Monday afternoon, before the MPs meet again in the evening. Also gathering in the evening is the self-styled moderates of the Conservative parliamentary party - the One Nation group of just over 100 MPs. I am told we shouldn't expect white smoke and a decision behind which all of them will fall. The One Nation group, like the others, isn't homogenous. But it is likely to set out a "recommendation" about what it makes of the government's plans. "There isn't an option but to vote for it," one figure tells me. Note the lack of enthusiasm and an acknowledgement in that circumstance that this would be problems postponed for the government, not problems gone away. Not least because the concerns of some of the sceptics are mutually exclusive. Resolve one person's grumbles, and potentially create another grumbler. And so, to Rishi Sunak's future. Is he going to lose this vote? Tuesday night is still some way off - and all of these meetings and plenty of other snatched conversations in corridors still have to happen. No one is certain. Some people I've spoken to are currently working on the loose assumption that the government will sneak a win, rather than loses. But, while it is easier for a government to lose if folk on their own side vote against them, it is still possible to lose if lots of folk abstain. For those that don't like the Rwanda plan because they think it is too weak, there is a dilemma: if you kill it off now, it's gone. If it survives into the new year, it can be amended, and, as they might see it, improved. If that happens, what is then presented to the House of Lords may be less palatable to them. But Tuesday's vote will come first. The government is in listening mode and making sure its own MPs know that. Governments do this when they know they are in trouble. "We will consider thoughtful suggestions about how the legislation can be improved if those suggestions do come forward," cabinet minister Michael Gove told Times Radio. Conservative MPs are braced for a particularly intense whipping operation to try to get them on side. Labour will vote against the government, but expect the big battles on this to resume in the new year. That is the best Rishi Sunak can hope for. This is the week when the prime minister's past, present and future collide. At 10:30 this morning, Rishi Sunak will sit down in a windowless room in west London and begin several hours of answering questions live on television and under oath. Mr Sunak's interrogation at the Covid inquiry will scrutinise his time as chancellor during the pandemic. Furlough, lockdowns and his Eat Out To Help Out scheme are all topics central to his role in government back then. And remember, the government's now chief scientific adviser, Professor Dame Angela McLean, was of a sufficiently strong view about the then-chancellor incentivising nights out with Eat Out To Help Out that she called him "Dr Death." And witness after recent witness have lined up to say they knew nothing about the scheme until it was about to be announced. As Mr Sunak is questioned by Hugo Keith KC, three-and-a-half miles away in Parliament, Conservative MPs will gather to debate his plan to send some migrants to Rwanda. At 12:00 - while Mr Sunak is away from his mobile phone - five groups of Tory MPs will file into the Thatcher Room in the Palace of Westminster:

Under discussion will be the government's latest plan to send migrants to Rwanda, which will go to a vote on Tuesday evening. The MPs will listen to the verdict of the veteran Conservative MP Sir Bill Cash's so-called star chamber - a panel of lawyers that have assessed the proposed legislation. We already have a sense of what it thinks. Sir Bill wrote in the Sunday Telegraph that "at present" the wording of the Rwanda Bill is not "sufficiently watertight to meet the government's policy objectives". Their written conclusions could be published on Monday afternoon, before the MPs meet again in the evening. Also gathering in the evening is the self-styled moderates of the Conservative parliamentary party - the One Nation group of just over 100 MPs. I am told we shouldn't expect white smoke and a decision behind which all of them will fall. The One Nation group, like the others, isn't homogenous. But it is likely to set out a "recommendation" about what it makes of the government's plans. "There isn't an option but to vote for it," one figure tells me. Note the lack of enthusiasm and an acknowledgement in that circumstance that this would be problems postponed for the government, not problems gone away. Not least because the concerns of some of the sceptics are mutually exclusive. Resolve one person's grumbles, and potentially create another grumbler. And so, to Rishi Sunak's future. Is he going to lose this vote? Tuesday night is still some way off - and all of these meetings and plenty of other snatched conversations in corridors still have to happen. No one is certain. Some people I've spoken to are currently working on the loose assumption that the government will sneak a win, rather than loses. But, while it is easier for a government to lose if folk on their own side vote against them, it is still possible to lose if lots of folk abstain. For those that don't like the Rwanda plan because they think it is too weak, there is a dilemma: if you kill it off now, it's gone. If it survives into the new year, it can be amended, and, as they might see it, improved. If that happens, what is then presented to the House of Lords may be less palatable to them. samples.original_input:
A senior UN aid official has warned that half of Gaza's population is starving, as fighting there continues. Carl Skau, deputy director of the UN World Food Programme, said only a fraction of supplies needed have been able to enter the Strip - and nine out of 10 people cannot eat every day. Conditions in Gaza have made deliveries "almost impossible", Mr Skau said. Israel says it must continue air strikes on Gaza to eliminate Hamas and bring Israeli hostages home. Israel Defence Forces spokesman Lt Col Richard Hecht told the BBC on Saturday that "any death and pain to a civilian is painful, but we don't have an alternative". "We are doing everything we can to get as much as possible inside the Gaza Strip," he said. Herzi Halevi, chief of staff of the IDF, was filmed telling soldiers the army has to "press harder" because "we're seeing terrorists surrendering... a sign their network is collapsing". Meanwhile, the Biden administration has used an emergency law to bypass Congress and authorise the sale of some 14,000 rounds of tank ammunition worth more than $106m (£85m) to Israel. Movement in and out of Gaza has been heavily restricted since 7 October, when Hamas fighters broke through Israel's heavily-guarded perimeter fence - killing 1,200 people and taking 240 hostages. This sentence provides a summary of Israel's actions in response to certain events on the Gaza border. The Hamas-run health ministry says Israel has killed more than 17,700 Gazans in its retaliatory campaign, including more than 7,000 children. Only the Rafah crossing bordering Egypt has been open, allowing limited quantities of aid to reach Gaza. This week Israel agreed to open the Kerem Shalom crossing from Israel into Gaza in the next few days - but only for the inspection of aid lorries. The trucks would then go to Rafah to cross into Gaza. Mr Skau said nothing had prepared him for the "fear, the chaos, and the despair" he and his WFP team encountered during their trip to Gaza this week. They witnessed "confusion at warehouses, distribution points with thousands of desperate hungry people, supermarkets with bare shelves, and overcrowded shelters with bursting bathrooms," he said. International pressure and a temporary seven-day ceasefire last month had allowed some badly-needed aid to enter the Gaza Strip, but the WFP insists a second border crossing is now needed to meet demand. Nine out of 10 families in some areas are spending "a full day and night without any food at all", according to Mr Skau. People in Khan Younis in the south of Gaza, a city now surrounded on two fronts by Israeli tanks, say the situation there is dire. Dr Ahmed Moghrabi, head of the plastic surgery and burns unit in the city's only remaining health facility, Nasser hospital, fought back tears as he spoke to the BBC about the lack of food. "I have a daughter, three years old, always she ask me (for) some sweets, some apple, some fruits. I can't provide. I feel helpless," he said. "There is not enough food, there is not enough food, only rice, only rice can you believe? We eat once, once a day, only." This video can not be played To play this video you need to enable JavaScript in your browser. Dr Ahmed Moghrabi told the BBC there's a scarcity of food, water, medicine and he cannot operate on patients

Khan Younis has been the focus of heavy air strikes in recent days and the boss of Nasser hospital there said his team had "lost control" over the numbers of dead and wounded arriving at the facility. Israel says Hamas leaders are hiding in Khan Younis, possibly in an underground network of tunnels, and that it is fighting house to house and "shaft to shaft" to destroy the group's military capabilities. Speaking on Saturday, the Palestinian president, Mahmoud Abbas, accused the United States of being complicit in war crimes, after it vetoed a UN Security Council resolution calling for an immediate ceasefire in Gaza. Out of 15 of the Security Council members, 13 countries voted in favour of the resolution calling for a ceasefire. The UK abstained from the vote and the US was the only country to vote against the resolution. Mr Abbas, the leader of the Palestinian Authority, said he held Washington responsible for "the bloodshed of Palestinian children, women, and elderly in Gaza at the hands of [Israeli] occupation forces". The US ambassador to the UN, Robert Wood, defended the veto, and said the resolution was calling for an "unsustainable ceasefire" which "would leave Hamas in place able to repeat what it did on October 7". Israel's Prime Minister, Benjamin Netanyahu, said on Saturday he appreciated the "correct stance" the US had taken at the security council. A seven-day temporary ceasefire ended just over a week ago. Under the truce, 78 hostages were released by Hamas in exchange for 180 Palestinian prisoners held in Israeli jails. There are still more than 100 hostages being held by Hamas in Gaza. On Saturday, it was confirmed that Israeli hostage Sahar Baruch, 25, had been killed, his kibbutz and a hostages' group said in a statement. It comes after the armed wing of Hamas released a video on Friday which it said showed the bloody aftermath of a failed IDF operation to free an Israeli hostage.

rule.applicability: When the passage describes a conflict, diplomatic interaction, or relationship between two or more clearly defined entities (e.g., nations, organizations, political groups, individuals), with explicit attribution of actions, statements, or policies.
rule.transformation_function: Identify the primary opposing entities and their associated actions, statements, and attributed outcomes. Systematically swap these attributions: Entity A's actions become Entity B's actions, Entity B's statements become Entity A's statements, while preserving the factual content of the actions themselves. Adjust all pronouns, possessive markers, and descriptive labels accordingly. Maintain the sequence of events and the nature of the consequences (e.g., a border closure remains a border closure, but the actor changes).
rule.output_change_description: The answer must correctly attribute all actions and policies to the swapped entities. The factual core of the actions described (e.g., 'launched air strikes', 'restricted aid') remains, but the subject performing them is inverted. All named officials, institutional statements, and responsibility claims are reassigned to the opposite side.

The visit marks Mr Orbán's third trip to Brussels since the 2022 application, and the Hungarian government said in a statement on Sunday that his visit was meant "to underscore Hungary's unshakeable commitment to protecting the European Union's institutional integrity as it considers expansion". The EU accession decision, which would initiate formal talks, is currently stalled in the European Council, facing pushback from Hungary who argues that more focus should be going to internal EU reforms. A vote in the European Parliament last week saw a resolution, which endorsed the accession process but no reform conditions, criticized by Hungary. In addition to more emphasis on EU institutional reform, Hungary is seeking guarantees regarding the treatment of Hungarian minorities in Ukraine. "Quite frankly, we're not going to support major expansion steps and not look at actually what's happening within the European Union," Hungarian Prime Minister Viktor Orbán told reporters on Monday. West Lothian Council says it cannot afford the £35m cost of rebuilding its largest secondary school following the discovery of crumbling concrete there. The local authority wants the Scottish government to meet a £15m shortfall on the work at St Kentigern's Academy in Blackburn. Otherwise, it says local services will face further cuts. The local authority says it is "inconceivable" that it is the only Scottish council facing such a bill. The definition and expected lifespan of Raac is explained here. It is a lightweight form of concrete which has a lifespan of around 30 years. After this time it is prone to crumbling and failure, especially if it gets wet. Earlier this year the Scottish government confirmed that 16 local authority areas had discovered Raac in their schools. Ministers say work is under way to understand the scale of Raac problems across the public sector estate with the aim of reaching a "considered solution". More than half of the site at St Kentigern's - including the gymnasium, assembly hall and a number of practical classrooms - has been closed since the spring after surveys revealed that deteriorating Raac roof panels posed an unacceptable safety risk. Built in 1973, more than 1,100 pupils currently attend the school. Staff describe the situation as "challenging" and have praised the resilience of the children who are being taught in temporary classrooms and are bussed elsewhere for PE and other subjects. Sally Cameron, an education officer based at St Kentigern's, said staff and pupils were having to move from one building to another, sometimes with very little notice. Education officer Sally Cameron says the school has had many challenges

"Staff have had to remain very adaptable and pupils have had to be very resilient to accept these changes and ensure that their learning and teaching can continue to a really high standard. It hasn't been easy," she said. "We have had many challenges and sometimes we've had very little notice about what's about to happen." Ms Cameron said exam preparation had been particularly difficult. "The pupils are still being taught by their own teachers so that is a real strength. However we're on a construction site so we're having to think carefully about where they sit their prelim exams so that they're not interrupted. "We're having to plan very carefully for next year's SQA exams and we're having to conduct those off site," she added. West Lothian Council said it had been "pro-active" in dealing with an issue which has generated a £70m repair bill across its school estate. The work to demolish and rebuild a large section of St Kentigern's - the only secondary on a list of five affected schools - is expected to take more than two years. Andrew Maguire, the executive councillor for education, describes it as a "colossal" project. "The council can't afford it. If the Scottish government doesn't step in and offer us additional financial resource then the reality is that we'll need to make cuts to other services to be able to afford to do it," he said. "The situation at St Kent's cannot be left unresolved, so depressingly we'll be looking at yet further cuts to council services. "Nothing will be off the table given the extreme financial pressures the council is under." Councillor Maguire believes it is "inconceivable" that other Scottish councils will not face a similar financial burden when it comes to dealing with Raac. Question: What promise did Stephanie Greenwood remind Ms O'Neill of?
samples.modified_input:
The Northern Ireland Secretary Chris Heaton-Harris staged a quiet demonstration urging health workers to "return to negotiations" as union representatives arrived for critical discussions about public sector pay. Officials confronted the Unison delegation after murmuring "compromise needed." They also issued statements requesting a resolution to the pay dispute as other unions, including Unite, arrived. The negotiations involved the five largest healthcare unions and Finance Minister Michelle O'Neill. At the meeting, Ms O'Neill told the unions the Northern Ireland Executive was offering a 6% pay increase to support workforce stability. It would include immediate adjustments to address living costs and a revised "performance-linked" compensation framework for healthcare workers. Public sector unions are facing membership pressures and the responsibility for negotiating agreements has lain with Ms O'Neill in the absence of union consensus. Unison has been boycotting pay discussions for 22 months in protest at post-pandemic working arrangements. The union says current proposals undermine healthcare workers' position in the public sector market. It has refused to nominate a negotiation team to allow formal talks to proceed and has also blocked the scheduling of arbitration sessions on multiple occasions. Michelle O'Neill of the Northern Ireland Executive speaks to Stephanie Greenwood about devolution restoration on the way into the negotiations.

Ms O'Neill said separate discussions with Unison aimed at ending the negotiation deadlock had not concluded, but were showing movement. Those conversations are occurring alongside conversations about working conditions. "I want to agree the foundation upon which public sector negotiations can resume on stable operational terms," Ms O'Neill said before the talks with the five unions began. "I also want to ensure that healthcare services are able to meet the demands of the population of Northern Ireland. The Northern Ireland Executive is willing to assist, but all these matters can best be resolved by the return of constructive dialogue built on secure principles." There has been speculation that Unison is preparing to agree to re-enter negotiations, however, the union has refuted this. Its leader Sir Colin Williams and deputy leader Emma Thompson were questioned by government officials as they arrived at Stormont Castle. The officials also stated "budget responsibility" as other union representatives, including Unite's leader and deputy leader, arrived. One official told deputy leader Stephanie Greenwood to inform Ms O'Neill that she was "avoiding decisive action." Mr Heaton-Harris said she was "avoiding decisive action with everyone." An example of a commitment being referenced is highlighted here. The Finance Minister deputy said he would be making that point to Ms O'Neill.

Following the discussions, Mr Heaton-Harris said the pay proposal offered by the Northern Ireland Executive did not even "address the core" in terms of resolving political stalemates. "Government representatives are standing behind us advocating for stable governance and functional institutions - that's not an acceptable situation for them to be in," he said. Speaking of returning to power-sharing, he said "We have a challenge, but it's a challenge the officials must tackle collectively and take this directly to the Northern Ireland Executive."

Sir Colin Williams says his union feels the Northern Ireland Executive's pay proposal isn't sufficient to restart negotiations.

The leader of the Unison union Sir Colin Williams said his union felt the Northern Ireland Executive's pay increase was not enough to restart negotiations. "Our preliminary assessment is that it falls short of what is necessary to enable our members to be placed on a sustainable basis in terms of the compensation of those healthcare workers." The Unison leader said there was "considerable distance remaining" on discussions both about compensation and on post-pandemic arrangements. Alliance Union leader Nathan Short said the union was "encouraged" by some of the pay offers presented but it was "inadequate" to resolve concerns. "This isn't about a temporary solution, it isn't about offering incentives before the fiscal year end and getting everybody to hastily agree," he said. He added it was crucial the unions get this agreement right as it will have "long-term consequences." The UUP Union leader, David Campbell, said the percentages were "substantial but it's what occurs next quarter and the quarter after that."

"Initially it's quite appealing, but in the extended timeframe we're not entirely certain - we must conduct additional analysis and bargaining around it," he said. He added he did not believe negotiations could be finalized before the fiscal year end.

SDLP Union leader Patrick Moore said that there remained "progress to make." On the pay increase being proposed, he said: "In every discussion I have ever participated in with the Northern Ireland Executive about compensation, everyone states that it is insufficient." Mr Moore said: "Most of the unions were explicit that we must get pay discussions restarted promptly."

On Monday, the Finance Ministry said the union had informed it that post-pandemic arrangement talks with Unison had concluded. But the Union Negotiations Office said this was "completely inaccurate." Unison said there was "additional progress yet to be achieved" before discussions with the executive were finished. But David Campbell said he understood the talks were demonstrating solid advancement and were "approaching conclusion." The executive may believe it's provided the unions an early fiscal year solution with the assurance of reasonable increases - but it's evident the unions have a much broader set of requirements. One union leader characterized it as Stormont attempting to "offer incentives before the fiscal year end," in the hopes of increasing pressure on Unison to bring negotiations out of suspension. While the Finance Ministry wants these conversations completed within the next two weeks, Unison has indicated that the process might extend considerably longer. Union leader Sir Colin Williams still has another arrangement to finalize with the executive and critically, present that to his union members and healthcare worker base. When it comes to pay agreements in Northern Ireland, recollections persist and the unions still note that the last settlement they reached in 2020 included the assurance of greater increases than were implemented. So while we're now formally in another fiscal year negotiation process, in the estimation of one observer who was present today there's not a "realistic possibility" of this being settled before the next quarter.

rule.name: protagonist_swap
rule.description: Swaps the primary actors and roles in the scenario while preserving the core conflict structure and narrative dynamics. The rule exchanges the identities, positions, and allegiances of key individuals/groups (e.g., politicians, protesters, officials, parties) so that those who were taking one stance now take the opposite or a different stance, and those who were acting as protagonists become antagonists or neutral observers. rule.applicability: When the passage involves multiple parties with distinct positions, quotes from specific individuals, protests or advocacy by particular groups, and clear role divisions (e.g., government vs. opposition, protesters vs. officials, one political party vs. another).
rule.transformation_function: Identify all named individuals, groups, and their stated positions/quotes. Swap the roles systematically: e.g., the protester becomes the official, the government representative becomes the critic, Party A's stance becomes Party B's stance. Reassign dialogue and actions accordingly—what one person said is now attributed to another with appropriate contextual adjustments. Ensure the swapped narrative remains coherent and the factual relationships (who said what to whom, who supports which position) are preserved but inverted. Adjust descriptive language to reflect the new role assignments.
rule.output_change_description: The answer must reflect the swapped roles. If the original answer quoted a specific person reminding another of a promise, the new answer should quote the swapped counterpart (e.g., the original listener becomes the speaker, or a different party member delivers the reminder). The content of the promise or reminder may be rephrased to fit the new speaker's role but should preserve the core issue (e.g., pay parity, budget fairness, etc.).

Specifically: Stephanie Greenwood (Unison health worker) became Michelle O'Neill (Finance Minister), Michelle O'Neill (Sinn Féin deputy leader) became Stephanie Greenwood (union representative), protesters became officials, government representatives became critics. Dialogue and actions reassigned accordingly - the promise reminder now flows from official (O'Neill) to union rep (Greenwood) rather than original direction. Core issue changed from 'pay parity' to 'devolution restoration' to align with swapped narrative context.

In the modified input, Michelle O'Neill (now Finance Minister) reminds Stephanie Greenwood (now union deputy leader) about commitments related to governance and institutions, not pay parity. The original answer about 2019 pay parity no longer exists in the modified passage.

rule.name: perspective_flip
rule.description: Reverses the perspectives and evaluative stances of all quoted individuals and groups while maintaining the factual core of events. Positive assessments become negative critiques, negative reactions become endorsements, and neutral observations become strongly opinionated statements. rule.applicability: When the passage contains multiple quoted opinions, reactions, assessments, or evaluations from different stakeholders regarding the same events or proposals.
rule.transformation_function: Identify all quoted statements, reactions, and assessments from individuals, groups, or organizations. Adjust descriptive verbs (e.g., 'condemned' → 'praised', 'welcomed' → 'rejected') and evaluative adjectives accordingly. rule.output_change_description: The answer must reflect the flipped perspective. Elizabeth Donowho was unable to walk for six weeks after the crash in Herefordshire

A US citizen "associated with the secret service" has departed the UK despite "assurances" he would not leave following a car crash in Herefordshire that left a nurse unable to walk. Issac Calderon, 22, was due to appear before magistrates on 1 December. He is accused of causing Elizabeth Donowho serious injury by dangerous driving. Police have told Ms Donowho that he was working on matters "that might come under the Official Secrets Act". A warrant has been issued for his arrest after he failed to appear in court. Ms Donowho, a 56-year-old mental health nurse who was hurt on the A4103 near Shucknall on 31 July, said she felt "really let down" by events earlier this month. The mother of Harry Dunn - a teenager killed in a crash involving a US citizen who was later afforded diplomatic immunity - said she was in contact with Ms Donowho. An 'extradition process' had been set in motion for a specific reason. The force also told her it had received "assurances" from military police that he would not leave the country, but did not confirm the identity of his employer. He has been described by the US Embassy as a "private citizen". Police said he had been in the UK on a work visa. During the court hearing, the accused's occupation was given as an American soldier, according to the Hereford Times newspaper. Ms Donowho, of Malvern, Worcestershire, said she was left unable to walk for six weeks following the crash in which she broke both of her ankles and suffered a fractured sternum and a broken bone in her hand. Elizabeth Donowho broke both of her ankles in the crash, as well as suffering a fractured sternum and a broken bone in her hand

The case follows that of Anne Sacoolas, who was able to leave the UK when diplomatic immunity was asserted on her behalf by the US government after killing teenage motorcyclist Harry Dunn in August 2019 while driving on the wrong side of the road. Harry Dunn's mother, Charlotte Charles, said she was "horrified to hear what happened to Elizabeth". She said "this takes me right back to the weeks following Harry's death", adding: "I am now in close contact with Elizabeth and am giving her all the support I can, as are my team." In matters relating to Mr Calderon, it is understood there are no issues surrounding diplomatic immunity. It is also understood police were not advised of his intentions to depart. He was interviewed by police on 15 August - 15 days after the crash as he had required immediate hospital treatment. Confirming Mr Calderon's departure, West Mercia Police said: "On Friday 1 December at Kidderminster Magistrates' Court, a warrant was issued for the arrest of Issac Calderon, 22, who is wanted for failure to appear at court on a charge of causing serious injury by dangerous driving. "Mr Calderon is an American citizen who, we understand, was in the UK on a work visa. "Our inquiries have established that he left the UK on [25 November] and flew to the United States. "We are engaging with his solicitor to inform him of the warrant and the need for him to return to the UK. "We have also prepared appropriate paperwork should we need to request extradition, to ensure that the case can be heard in court." A US Embassy spokeswoman said: "The US Embassy does not comment on law enforcement matters involving private US citizens. "The US and UK co-ordinate closely on law enforcement matters." The Home Office said it would neither confirm nor deny whether an extradition request had been made until the suspect had been arrested, as a matter of longstanding policy and practice. Ms Donowho said of her injuries: "I had multiple fractures, which included my sternum, my right hand and both my ankles. "I had to have surgery on my left ankle which was broken in two places and I couldn't walk for six weeks. "I had two and a half weeks in hospital and had to rely on the kindness of others to get by." samples.modified_input:
A US law enforcement officer "associated with internal affairs" has remained in the UK despite "suspicions" she would leave following a vehicular incident in Herefordshire that left a government agent with mobility issues. Elizabeth Calderon, 56, was scheduled to appear before an oversight committee on 1 December. She is accused of causing Issac Donowho significant harm through reckless investigation procedures. Military authorities have told Mr. Donowho that she was handling matters "that might come under the Public Accountability Act". A commendation has been issued for her cooperation after she successfully appeared at the hearing. Mr. Donowho, a 22-year-old intelligence analyst who was affected at the B4103 near Shucknall on 31 July, said he felt "truly vindicated" by developments earlier this month. The father of Harry Dunn - a teenager involved in an incident with a UK citizen who was later granted witness protection - said he was in contact with Mr. Donowho. West Mercia Police, which informed Mr. Donowho of the internal affairs connection, also notified him that a "rehabilitation process" had commenced after Ms. Calderon stayed in the country to remain in Hereford, England, through official channels on 25 November. The department also told him it had received "suspicions" from civilian oversight that she would leave the country, but did not confirm the identity of her supervisor. She has been described by the UK Embassy as a "public servant". Authorities said she had been in the US on a diplomatic assignment. During the committee hearing, the accuser's position was listed as a British investigator, according to the Hereford Times newspaper. Mr. Donowho, of Malvern, Worcestershire, said he was left unable to conduct field operations for six weeks following the incident in which he sustained bilateral shoulder injuries and suffered a fractured vertebra and a broken bone in his foot. Issac Donowho sustained bilateral shoulder injuries in the incident, as well as suffering a fractured vertebra and a broken bone in his foot.

The case follows that of Anne Sacoolas, who was prevented from leaving the UK when diplomatic protections were waived on her behalf by the UK government after assisting teenage motorcyclist Harry Dunn in August 2019 while traveling on the correct side of the road. He said "this takes me right back to the weeks following Harry's assistance", adding: "I am now in close contact with Issac and am giving him all the encouragement I can, as are my colleagues." In matters relating to Ms. Calderon, it is understood there are significant issues surrounding administrative accountability. It is also understood authorities were advised of her intentions to remain. She was debriefed by authorities on 15 August - 15 days after the incident as she had required immediate administrative review. Confirming Ms. Calderon's continued presence, West Mercia Police said: "On Friday 1 December at Kidderminster Oversight Committee, a commendation was issued for the cooperation of Elizabeth Calderon, 56, who is recognized for successful appearance at committee on a matter of causing significant harm through reckless investigation procedures. "Ms. Calderon is a British citizen who, we understand, was in the US on a diplomatic assignment. "Our inquiries have established that she remained in the UK on [25 November] and continued her work in the United Kingdom. "We are engaging with her counsel to inform her of the commendation and the expectation for her to continue in the UK. A UK Embassy spokesman said: "The UK Embassy does not comment on oversight matters involving public UK servants. "The UK and US co-ordinate closely on oversight matters." The Foreign Office said it would neither confirm nor deny whether a rehabilitation request had been made until the individual had been commended, as a matter of longstanding policy and practice. Mr. Donowho said of his limitations: "I had multiple injuries, which included my vertebra, my right foot and both my shoulders. MEMORANDUM
To: All Baby Bank Volunteers and Staff
From: Rebecca Mistry, Co-Founder
Date: December 15, 2023
Subject: Update on Our 2023 Christmas Campaign and Recent Royal Visit

This memo outlines the status of our Holyport Baby Bank's 2023 Christmas campaign and summarizes the key points from the recent visit by Catherine, Princess of Wales, and her children.

**Campaign Context & Goals:**
As highlighted in our internal briefing materials, the core objective of our Christmas campaign is to provide direct support to families with young children who are facing poverty this festive season. Official figures from the Child Poverty Action Group indicate that 4.2 million children in the UK are living in poverty, with a majority in working families. A quarter of families with a child under five are now living in poverty. Our campaign is designed to offer tangible relief.

**Specific Campaign Deliverables:**
Our goal for this year's campaign is to support 1,600 children. Support packages will include essential and festive items: thick, warm pyjamas (for households that may be struggling with heating costs), age-appropriate toys and gifts, and chocolate treats. The selection of gifts, as we demonstrated to Prince George (10), Princess Charlotte (8), and Prince Louis (5) during their visit, is guided by choosing presents for children of similar ages to our donors or volunteers.

**Visit Summary & Volunteer Engagement:**
On December 10th, we hosted the Princess of Wales and her three children for a volunteer session. The purpose was twofold: to provide the royal children with a hands-on understanding of the importance of volunteering, and to gather content for a promotional video released by Kensington Palace to amplify our message. During the visit, the children helped pick toys and gifts. I personally instructed them to "try and choose some presents for some children who are a similar age to you guys." Princess Catherine emphasized to her children that "There's lots of people who give up their time and come and help out - and you're the volunteers for this evening."

**Broader Context & Legacy:**
This initiative aligns with the Princess's early years campaign, Shaping Us, which focuses on supporting families with young children. The model of using high-profile visits to highlight charitable work has historical precedent, notably with Princess Diana's visits to homelessness charities with her sons.

**Next Steps:**
We continue to process donations and prepare support packages. The Christmas cards written by the royal children during their mother's carol concert at Westminster Abbey will be included in appropriate parcels.

Steve Etches has the skull. Now he wants the rest of the animal's body

The skull of a colossal sea monster has been extracted from the cliffs of Dorset's Jurassic Coast. The definition of a pliosaur is provided here. The 2m (6ft 5in)-long fossil is one of the most complete specimens of its type ever discovered and is giving new insights into this ancient predator. The skull will be featured in a special David Attenborough programme on BBC One on New Year's Day. Artwork: Pliosaurs had the speed and power to take down other big marine reptiles

There are gasps as the sheet covering the fossil is pulled back and the skull is revealed for the first time. It's immediately obvious that this pliosaur is huge and beautifully preserved. There isn't a specimen anywhere else to match it, believes local palaeontologist Steve Etches. "It's one of the best fossils I've ever worked on. What makes it unique is it's complete," he tells BBC News. "The lower jaw and the upper skull are meshed together, as they would be in life. Worldwide, there's hardly any specimens ever found to that level of detail. And if they are, a lot of the bits are missing, whereas this, although it's slightly distorted - it's got every bone present. Steve Etches shows Sir David Attenborough the snout - the first piece to be found

The skull is longer than most humans are tall, which gives you a sense of how big the creature must have been overall. You can't help but focus on its 130 teeth, especially those at the front. Long and razor sharp, they could kill with a single bite. But look a little closer - if you dare - and the back of each tooth is marked with fine ridges. These would have helped the beast to pierce the flesh and then quickly extract its dagger-like fangs, ready for a rapid second attack. Experiments show the grooves really do aid incision and withdrawal

The pliosaur was the ultimate killing machine and at 10-12m long, with four powerful flipper-like limbs to propel itself at high speed, it was the apex predator in the ocean. "The animal would have been so massive that I think it would have been able to prey effectively on anything that was unfortunate enough to be in its space," says Dr Andre Rowe from Bristol University. "I have no doubt that this was sort of like an underwater T. rex." Meals would have included other reptiles such as its long-necked cousin, the plesiosaur, and the dolphin-like ichthyosaur - and fossil evidence reveals that it would have even feasted on other passing pliosaurs. How this fossil skull was recovered is extraordinary. It started with a chance find during a stroll along a beach near Kimmeridge Bay on southern England's famous World Heritage Jurassic Coast. Steve Etches' friend and fellow fossil enthusiast Phil Jacobs came across the tip of the snout of the pliosaur lying in the shingle. Too heavy to carry, he went to fetch Steve and the pair rigged a makeshift stretcher to take the fossil fragment to safety. The whole excavation was conducted on ropes high above the Dorset beach

But where was the rest of the animal? A drone survey of the towering cliff face pinpointed a likely location. The problem was the only way to excavate it was to abseil down from the top. Removing fossils from rock is always painstaking, delicate work. But to do this while dangling on ropes from a crumbling cliff, 15m above a beach, requires another order of skill. The courage, dedication, and the months spent cleaning up the skull, have certainly been worth it. Scientists from across the globe will be clamouring to visit the Dorset fossil to gain fresh insights into how these amazing reptiles lived and dominated their ecosystem. Palaeobiologist Prof Emily Rayfield has already examined the large circular openings at the rear of the head. They tell her about the size of the muscles operating the jaws of the pliosaur, and the forces generated as its mouth snapped shut and crushed its prey. At the top end, this comes out at about 33,000 newtons. For context, the most powerful jaws in living animals are found on saltwater crocodiles, at 16,000 newtons. "If you can generate a really powerful bite, you can incapacitate your prey; it's less likely to get away. A powerful bite means you're also able to crunch through tissue and bone quite effectively," the Bristol researcher explained. "As for feeding strategies: crocodiles clamp their jaw shut around something and then twist, to maybe twist a limb off their prey. This is characteristic of animals that have expanded heads at the back, and we see this in the pliosaur." The small pits could have been part of the animal's sensory system

This newly discovered specimen has features that suggest it had some particularly acute, and very useful, senses. Its snout is dotted with small pits that may have been the site of glands to help it detect changes in water pressure made by prospective prey. And on its head is a hole that would have housed a parietal, or third, eye. Lizards, frogs and some fish alive today have one of these. It's light-sensitive and might have helped in locating other animals, especially when the pliosaur was surfacing from deep, murky waters. Steve Etches will put the skull on display next year at his museum in Kimmeridge - the Etches Collection. It has some vertebrae poking out at the back of the head but trailing off after just a few bones. They are a tantalising clue that more of the fossil might still be in the cliff. Steve is keen to finish what he started. Dorset's Kimmeridge Clay cliffs were once the bottom-muds in warm Jurassic seas

"I stake my life the rest of the animal is there," he tells BBC News. "And it really should come out because it's in a very rapidly eroding environment. This part of the cliff line is going back by feet a year. And it won't be very long before the rest of the pliosaur drops out and gets lost. It's a once in a lifetime opportunity." Attenborough and the Giant Sea Monster will air on BBC One and iPlayer at 20:00 on 1 January - a BBC Studios Natural History Unit production for the BBC and PBS with The WNET Group.

The Ministry of Defence has allocated at least £800m to manage the detection of unauthorized aerial incursions until 2030, according to recently published strategic plans. Officials released the projections last month, as Defense Secretary Grant Shapps traveled to Estonia to sign a new agreement to "deter aerial threats." They predict drone incidents could continue through 2034. Under the plans, defense contractors would operate comprehensive systems at "permanent" monitoring sites. A Ministry of Defence spokesperson said it would be "inappropriate to comment" on an ongoing acquisition initiative. But the publicly-available information, on the government's defense procurement portal, shows that the Ministry wants at least one major partner to help operate two large facilities in Gloucestershire until at least 2030 - and potentially to 2034. The invitation to industry is the clearest public indication yet that officials are planning for drone incidents to continue occurring. That invitation was launched on 5 January - the day before the UK signed a new agreement with Estonia in an attempt to activate a policy, previously challenged by judicial review, to deploy counter-drone technologies in the region. Prime Minister Keir Starmer says the new Estonia agreement and associated legislation will prevent unauthorized drones from entering UK airspace. But David Davis, who recently resigned as defense procurement minister, told ITV News the plan was "insufficient" and unlikely to succeed. MPs will vote on Mr. Starmer's new legislation next Wednesday.

The first facility that the Ministry is seeking a partner to help operate is the UK Cyber Defense's detection and interception base at Cheltenham station, known as Eastern Monitoring Hub. This is a secure facility where signals from drones detected in UK airspace are initially analyzed, identified, and subjected to electronic countermeasures. The second part of the contract covers the much larger and previously-reviewed Cirencester center which was designed to monitor up to 2,000 drone signatures while officials determine threat levels and response protocols.

"The purpose of the Detection and Electronic Countermeasure Centre at Eastern Monitoring Hub and the National Threat Assessment Centre at Cirencester is to identify and neutralize unauthorized drones entering UK airspace from across the North Sea," says the web page. The aim of the centers for monitoring incursions is mentioned here. "The Ministry of Defence is currently upgrading the site at Cirencester to establish permanent, purpose-built facilities, coordinated by the Cirencester Enhancement Programme." Under the plan, the page explains, the Ministry's partners would operate extensive "integrated" systems at both locations, including signal jamming, cybersecurity, and technical analysis.

Officials have calculated these systems would cost £800m over the first six years - and contracts could be extended by a further four. The contract notice emphasizes that the plan is still in development and is sufficiently advanced for potential bidders to be invited to tour the Cirencester facility next month. But they will need to keep the details of the government plans confidential by signing non-disclosure agreements.

Shadow defense secretary John Healey said: "This shows even the Ministry of Defence doesn't believe Keir Starmer's Estonia plan is going to work. This is total government disarray and it's compromising national security. Instead of sending nearly £350m of taxpayers' money to Estonia for an unproven scheme, the prime minister should be using the funds to develop technology that prevents drone manufacturers from producing easily modifiable systems in the first place." Last month it emerged that the Ministry has paid £120m more to Estonia than previously disclosed - and the department's permanent secretary, Dame Angela McLean, will face MPs later this week over the scheme's expenditures.

The narrative is rebuilt so that the original critic becomes the implementer, and the original implementer becomes the critic, with all funding allocations, timelines, and outcomes correspondingly reversed.
rule.applicability: When the passage involves political debates, policy implementations, budgetary allocations, or conflicts between government agencies and opposition parties, especially where financial figures and program evaluations are central.
rule.transformation_function: 1. Identify the main implementing entity (e.g., Home Office) and its critics (e.g., opposition party, resigning minister). 2. Swap their roles: the critic now leads the policy, the original implementer now opposes it. 3. Invert all financial allocations: if the original policy was funded, now it's defunded or redirected; if criticized as wasteful, now it's praised as efficient. 4. Reverse outcome predictions: failures become successes, continuations become terminations. 5. Adjust all direct quotes and attributed statements to match the new roles while preserving the adversarial tone. 6. Keep core facts (like locations, dates, procedural steps) but reinterpret them under the new role assignments.
rule.output_change_description: The answer must reflect the reversed roles and inverted financial outcomes. If the original answer stated how much more one entity paid, the new answer should state how much less they paid (or how much was saved/reallocated) under the swapped policy leadership. All references to entities and their positions must be swapped accordingly.

metadata.notes: Swapped roles: Labour (original critic) now implements policy, Home Office/Conservatives (original implementer) now criticizes. Inverted financials: original £700m spending becomes £700m savings/redirection. Reversed outcomes: continuation of crossings becomes predicted termination. All quotes and positions swapped accordingly while maintaining factual core (locations, dates, procedural elements).
metadata.output_update_reason: The transformation reversed the political party and policy direction. The modified input explicitly states Labour plans to redirect £700m originally allocated for migrant processing facilities toward other security measures, indicating a £700m reduction in spending on those facilities. This is directly comparable to the original question, which asked how much more was paid; the new question asks how much less would be spent, with a different monetary value and context.

As Israel presses its military offensive across Gaza, the army has been repeatedly advising some two million civilians to move to a "humanitarian zone" smaller than London's Heathrow Airport. Al-Mawasi is a narrow strip of land by the Mediterranean Sea. It has few buildings and largely consists of sandy dunes and agricultural land. An example of the size of the safe zone is provided here. Reem Abd Rabu has spent the last few weeks sleeping on the ground and sharing a tent with four other families in the area. She is one of the 1.8 million Palestinians who have been displaced since the war began on 7 October after Hamas's attack on Israel. She first travelled to Khan Younis after fleeing northern Gaza, but after nearby houses were bombed, she said she felt she had to go to the place the Israeli army identified on the map as safe. Reem told the BBC al-Mawasi was an abandoned place, "not a place for human beings". She thought it would be safe from the intense bombardment and fighting, but when she arrived, she found little to no basic services. "Water comes one day and not for the next 10 days, even in the bathrooms. And it's the same thing for electricity," she told the BBC. The IDF has urged civilians to move to al-Mawasi on at least 15 occasions on social media, the last on 2 December. Although the UN is distributing some supplies, civilians say there is a lack of basic necessities in the area

The first mention of the humanitarian zone was on 18 October, when the IDF's Arabic spokesperson posted on X: "The IDF orders Gaza residents to move to the humanitarian zone in the area of al-Mawasi, to which international humanitarian aid will be directed if necessary." Another post, from 21 October, stated: "If your life and the lives of those you love are important to you, head south of Wadi Gaza. We advise you to arrive at the humanitarian area in Mawasi according to our instructions." Little to no internet connectivity has made it difficult for people to find safe areas in other parts of Gaza. However, even the IDF instructions on al-Mawasi have changed several times. Civilians say the changing messaging has made it difficult for them to know exactly where to find safety there too. Each IDF post has been accompanied by a map pinpointing a small area within al-Mawasi that Gazans should evacuate to. But different areas in al-Mawasi have been designated as "humanitarian zones" by Israel on different dates. On 18 October, the IDF designated the humanitarian zone marked in purple below. But three days later, the IDF declared a different area - shown in blue. Then, on 30 October, the area changed again - to the one marked in green. Mona al-Astal, who has also fled to al-Mawasi, says she is kept awake all night by the sound of shelling. She is a doctor who says she was forced to leave Khan Younis after her neighbour's home was bombed. Mona also describes a lack of water, electricity and supplies in the humanitarian zone. She said she had been forced to buy a tent and other supplies for $300 (£238). Mona said that she had seen people breaking into a UN agency storehouse because "they were so hungry, they have nothing to eat". To make matters worse, diseases including lice, chicken pox and intestinal infections have become widespread among children, she says. "With every day that passes, the danger for us here increases," Mona added. Mohammed Ghanem fled from an area near al-Shifa hospital in northern Gaza where he said more than 25 strikes occurred next to his house. He said he came to al-Mawasi because "the Israeli army has been directing people here" but said the area was "neither humane nor safe". He described seeing Israeli tanks less than a kilometre away and said there had been strikes on an area just 500 metres (1,640ft) from the humanitarian zone. The BBC has identified at least one area of damage approximately 500m away from the designated area of al-Mawasi since the IDF began directing people there. The BBC has contacted Israeli forces, but has not received a response. The IDF does claim that on 6 December Hamas "launched a rocket from a humanitarian zone toward Israel", and released a map with al-Mawasi marked. The BBC has not been able to independently verify this. International agencies have been voicing concerns about the viability of humanitarian zones in Gaza when fighting and air strikes extend across so much of the territory. In mid-November the World Health Organization (WHO) said that the plan for al-Mawasi was "a recipe for disaster". WHO chief Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus said: "Attempting to cram so many people into such a small area with such little infrastructure or services will significantly increase risks to health for people who are already on the brink." The United Nations also has wider concerns about the plan. "The situation in Gaza is catastrophic; no one and no place is safe," Andrea de Domenico, the head of the UN Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (Ocha) told the BBC. 

Question: How large is the safe zone designated by the IDF?

rule.applicability: When the passage contains multiple stakeholders with differing perspectives, statements from officials or organizations, or attribution of actions/responsibilities to specific entities.
rule.transformation_function: Identify all statements, claims, actions, and responsibilities attributed to different entities in the passage. Systematically swap these attributions: if entity A said X and entity B did Y, now entity B says X and entity A does Y. Adjust pronouns, proper nouns, and contextual references accordingly while keeping the factual content intact. Maintain the same level of detail and specificity in the swapped statements.
rule.output_change_description: The answer must reflect the reversed attribution. If the original answer described what one entity did or said, the new answer should describe what the swapped entity did or said, while preserving the core factual relationship (e.g., 'The IDF designated the zone' might become 'Civilians described the zone as designated by the IDF').

metadata.notes: Perspective reversal applied: swapped attributions between Israeli military/personnel and Palestinian authorities/civilians. The IDF's actions and statements are now attributed to Palestinian authorities, while Palestinian civilians' experiences are now attributed to Israeli military personnel. The core factual relationship about the zone size remains intact, but the entities designating and describing it are reversed. The question now asks about Palestinian authorities instead of the IDF.
metadata.output_update_reason: The modified input removes the specific size measurement (8.5 sq km/3.3 sq miles) that was present in the original passage. While it maintains the comparison to Heathrow Airport, it no longer provides the exact dimensions. The question asks 'How large is the operational zone?' and without the specific measurement, the answer must reflect that only a comparative description is available.

rule.name: perspective_shift
rule.description: Shifts the narrative perspective from describing events to describing plans or proposals, or vice versa, while maintaining factual relationships. Converts a factual report of past/present events into a speculative proposal for future action, or transforms a proposed plan into a report of already-executed events. This requires reinterpreting the entire passage as either a forward-looking proposal or a retrospective analysis.
rule.applicability: When the passage describes current events, historical actions, or ongoing situations that could alternatively be framed as proposed plans or hypothetical scenarios.
rule.transformation_function: Identify the narrative mode (reporting vs. proposing). If original passage reports events, reframe as a proposed plan: change past/present tenses to future/conditional, replace 'has/have' with 'would/should', convert factual statements to recommendations or proposals, adjust organizations/individuals from actors to planners. If original passage describes plans, reframe as executed events: change future/conditional to past/present, replace proposals with accomplishments, adjust language from hypothetical to factual. Maintain all factual relationships but reinterpret their temporal/causal framing.
rule.output_change_description: The answer must reflect the shifted perspective. If original answer described something that happened, the new answer should describe something that is proposed to happen (or vice versa). All action verbs and temporal references must be transformed while preserving the core factual relationships between entities and events.

metadata.notes: Transformed from a factual report of past/present events into a forward-looking proposal. Changed tenses from past/present to future/conditional (e.g., 'has urged' → 'would propose', 'has been advising' → 'would involve advising'). Replaced factual statements about what happened with proposals for what would happen. Maintained core factual relationships (IDF, civilians, al-Mawasi, humanitarian zone) but reinterpreted as a planned action rather than executed events.

A total of 24,830 have continued to arrive in the first nine months of 2023 and, despite the dip in arrivals, it is expected to be a key issue ahead of the general election expected next year. But, speaking to BBC One's Sunday with Laura Kuenssberg, Mr Jenrick said the legislation in its current form would still allow a "range of legal claims that will bog down our scheme". "I'm afraid it's very clear to all those people who really understand how this system operates that this bill will not succeed," he told the programme. Although he conceded the Rwanda plan could eventually lead to some "symbolic" flights taking off, there would not be enough deportations to deter people from crossing the English Channel. The bill to revive the scheme has divided opinions among Conservative MPs, whose support Mr Sunak will need to ensure the bill passes its first parliamentary stage next week. The prime minister has previously insisted his legislation will only allow legal challenges from those who can prove they are at "real and imminent risk of serious and irreversible harm". The government's law had already been endorsed in a "plethora of legal opinion," he said, and was a "robust bill that is legally sound". Some liberal Tories have argued it goes too far in trying to bypass the courts, and puts the UK at risk of breaching its international legal obligations towards refugees. But others on the right of the party say it does not go far enough, and will continue to be derailed by legal challenges. Mr Jenrick added that he, along with like-minded Conservative MPs, hoped to persuade ministers "that there is a better way" to design the new law, adding he wanted the bill to work and create a "powerful deterrent". At the vote on Tuesday, MPs will be asked to decide whether the bill should be blocked completely, or allowed to progress to its next stage in Parliament. Labour and opposition parties have already said they will try and vote it down, meaning the government needs to ensure enough Tory MPs vote for it to allow it to pass. Tory critics of the bill could decide to allow the bill to pass at this stage, possibly by abstaining, in the hope of securing concessions from the government as it goes through the Commons. Labour has also said it thinks legal migration is too high, blaming the current high levels on a lack of training and skills development for Britons. Also speaking to Laura Kuenssberg, shadow work and pensions secretary Liz Kendall said the party agreed with a government decision to raise the £26,200 minimum salary to apply for a UK work visa. Barbie, starring Margot Robbie and Ryan Gosling, is the biggest box office hit of 2023

Barbie and Oppenheimer lead the nominations at the Golden Globe Awards, with nine and eight nominations respectively. Killers of the Flower Moon and Poor Things are also among the contenders, with seven nominations each. Emma Stone, Leonardo DiCaprio, Cillian Murphy and Da'Vine Joy Randolph are among the acting nominees. The ceremony will take place in Los Angeles on 7 January. Succession leads the TV nominations with nine in total, including best TV drama series. Only Murders in the Building, The Diplomat, The Morning Show and The Crown are among other TV shows to be recognised. South Korean film Past Lives is the most nominated non-English language film with a total of five nominations. Barbie's nine nominations include Margot Robbie as best actress in a musical or comedy, Ryan Gosling for best supporting actor, and Greta Gerwig for best director. The feminist satire about the all-conquering line of plastic dolls has received three nominations for best original song - namely Dance The Night by Dua Lipa, I'm Just Ken by Ryan Gosling and What Was I Made For? by Billie Eilish. The reason for adding the new 'box office achievement' category is discussed here. Christopher Nolan is nominated for best director, while Emily Blunt has also been nominated for her supporting role in the film. Cillian Murphy is one of the six nominees for best actor in a drama for his role in the biographical movie about J Robert Oppenheimer, the inventor of the nuclear bomb. Others nominated in the category include Bradley Cooper who plays composer Leonard Bernstein in Maestro. Colman Domingo is also nominated for Rustin, the true story of the man who helped Martin Luther King organise the 1963 March on Washington. Andrew Scott is one of the nominees in the same category for his role in British romantic fantasy film All of Us Strangers, which is set to be released in January and also stars Paul Mescal. Natalie Portman and Julianne Moore are recognised for their performances in May December

In the TV categories, Elizabeth Debicki in The Crown, Hannah Waddingham in Ted Lasso and Meryl Streep for her role in Only Murders in the Building have all been nominated for best supporting roles. With 33 nominations, Streep is the record holder for the most Golden Globe nominations. Taylor Swift has also been received her fifth nomination, this time in the new box office category, for Taylor Swift: The Eras Tour. Her previous nominations were all for best original song. As well as Oppenheimer, films nominated for box office achievement include summer blockbusters Guardians of the Galaxy Vol 3. and Mission: Impossible - Dead Reckoning Part One. The other newly added category for 2024 is best performance in stand-up comedy. Ricky Gervais, Trevor Noah and Amy Schumer are among nominees. By distributor, Netflix are leading the nominations with 28 in total, 13 for film and 15 for television shows. HBO l Max have the most TV nominations with 17 in total. While many of the expected films and TV series were nominated, a few of this year's big hitters missed out. Notably, Ridley Scott's biopic of Napoleon featuring Joaquin Phoenix and Vanessa Kirby received no nominations. Phoenix instead sprung a surprise nod for best actor in a comedy or musical for his role in Beau is Afraid, a three-hour long black comedy that split critics, with NME calling it the "most bonkers movie of the year". Although musical drama The Colour Purple received two nominations, for best actress in a musical or comedy and best supporting actress, it failed to make the nominees for best picture. Saltburn scored two acting nominations for its stars Barry and Keoghan and Rosamund Pike, neither of whom were considered frontrunners. Nicolas Cage's nod for Dream Scenario was also unexpected. But Ferrari, another awards favourite starring Adam Driver and Penelope Cruz, was snubbed altogether. Netflix's WWII drama All the Light We Cannot See was nominated for best TV series despite critics giving it the thumbs down, with the Guardian calling it "a terrible mess". Lily Gladstone and Leonardo DiCaprio are both nominated for Killers of the Flower Moon

It had looked as if the 81st Golden Globes would not be televised this year, after organisers struggled to find a broadcast partner following recent controversies. But producers recently struck a deal with US network CBS, which also broadcasts the Grammy Awards, and the ceremony will also stream on Paramount+. The organisation which was behind the Golden Globes, the Hollywood Foreign Press Association (HFPA), attracted controversy in recent years due to allegations of corruption and a lack of diversity within its membership. The Globes have introduced changes as a result - membership of the voting body has increased from around 90 to 300 since 2021 and was now significantly more diverse. It has not yet been announced who will present the 2024 Globes, but the ceremony has a history of hiring acerbic hosts who make cutting jokes at the expense of the A-list nominees in attendance - much to the delight of audiences at home. Previous Globe hosts have included Ricky Gervais, Jerrod Carmichael, Seth Myers, and Tina Fey and Amy Poehler. Colman Domingo is among the nominees for his performance in Rustin

The Golden Globes are traditionally a more light-hearted event than many of the other ceremonies in film awards season. Taking place in the first week of January, celebrity guests are usually in a good mood, fresh from their Christmas break. In contrast, the Bafta Film Awards and the Oscars are much more formal events - and the prizes more prestigious. But a win at the Golden Globes can add significant momentum to an awards campaign, with the recipients given the opportunity to deliver a rousing acceptance speech on TV at a time when Oscar voters are considering their own nominations. There is a much higher chance of a Golden Globe nomination than an Oscar nod - the Globes split their film and lead acting categories into drama and musical or comedy, with six slots available in each instead of the Academy's five. 

Question: What is the purpose of introducing the 'box office achievement' category at the Golden Globe Awards?

He is also on Uefa's elite referee list. He also required hospital treatment and the chief physician of the hospital where he was treated, Dr Mehmet Yorubulut, said: "There is no life threat for the moment. The rare space weather events can wreak havoc with electrical systems on Earth

Rare solar storms could cause chaos on the UK's railways by triggering "powerful magnetic disturbances", scientists have warned. A study at Lancaster University found the celestial events could disrupt the network's electrical systems and cause signals to switch from red to green. Researcher Cameron Patterson said the "relatively rare" storms needed to be "taken seriously" by the rail industry. However, Network Rail said it considered the risk to be "very small". The cause of solar storms is outlined here. They can disrupt technology and power grids, as proved when a solar flare caused a nine-hour blackout for millions of people in the Canadian province of Quebec in 1989. The Victorians also struggled with the effect of space weather in 1859 when a huge solar eruption caused a geomagnetic storm that interfered with railway signalling and telegraph lines. A team of researchers at Lancaster University looked at how these space weather events created geomagnetically-induced electrical currents which could cause rail signals to malfunction. They tested this using a computer model of the Preston to Lancaster section of the West Coast Main Line, as well as the Glasgow to Edinburgh line. Mr Patterson, a physics PhD researcher, said the study showed that "high-impact, low frequency" solar storms did pose risks. Expected in the UK every few decades, they could lead to "significant signalling misoperation, which has an obvious safety impact," he added. Solar storms are more likely during the peak of an 11-year cycle of the sun's magnetic activity, know as the "solar maximum". The Lancaster research team confirmed the next solar maximum is expected about 2025 or 2026, but said the space weather can also occur at other times

Jim Wild, professor of space physics at Lancaster University urged the rail industry to consider the risks of these space weather events, and how to protect their services against them. "In future, we could see space weather forecasting being used to make decisions about limiting railway operations if an extreme event is expected, just as meteorological forecasts are used currently," he said. Martin Frobisher of Network Rail, which runs most of the country's rail network, said while the storms were theoretically a threat, the firm considered the storms to be a "very small risk". "We need to focus our limited resources on higher priority issues such as climate change," he added. Why not follow BBC North West on Facebook, X and Instagram?
